title: Introduction to Program Evaluation
summary: A foundational overview of program evaluation methods, covering logic models, theory of change, and how to frame evaluation questions. Ideal for teams new to formal evaluation practice. Discusses formative vs. summative evaluation and when to use each approach.
transcript: Welcome to our introduction to program evaluation. Today we'll cover the fundamental concepts that every evaluator needs to understand. Program evaluation is the systematic collection of information about the activities, characteristics, and outcomes of programs to make judgments about the program, improve or further develop program effectiveness, inform decisions about future programming, and increase understanding. A logic model is a graphic representation of a program that shows the logical relationships between the resources that are invested, the activities that take place, and the changes or results that follow. Theory of change describes how and why a set of activities is expected to lead to early, intermediate, and long-term outcomes. Formative evaluation is conducted during program implementation to improve the program. Summative evaluation is conducted at the end of a program to assess effectiveness. Key evaluation questions should be specific, answerable, and tied to program goals. Data collection methods include surveys, interviews, focus groups, observation, and administrative data review.

title: Data Collection Strategies for Nonprofits
summary: Practical strategies for collecting high-quality data in nonprofit settings, including survey design, interview protocols, and managing data from multiple sites. Special focus on low-resource environments and volunteer data collectors.
transcript: Data collection is the foundation of any good evaluation. In this session we explore practical strategies for nonprofits operating with limited resources. Survey design best practices include keeping surveys short, using clear language, avoiding double-barreled questions, and piloting before full deployment. For interviews and focus groups, developing a strong protocol is essential. Open-ended questions allow participants to share their experiences in their own words. Probing questions help gather deeper information. When managing data from multiple sites, standardization is critical. Create clear data dictionaries, train all data collectors consistently, and build in quality checks. Administrative data, such as program records and databases, can be a rich source of information. Consider what data your organization already collects and how it can be used for evaluation purposes. Consent and confidentiality are paramount in all data collection activities.

title: Using Data to Tell Your Story
summary: How to transform raw evaluation data into compelling narratives for funders, boards, and communities. Covers data visualization principles, report writing, and communicating findings to non-technical audiences.
transcript: Data storytelling is the art of translating numbers and findings into narratives that resonate with your audience. In this webinar we focus on practical techniques for communicating evaluation results effectively. Start by knowing your audience: a board presentation requires different framing than a funder report or a community meeting. Data visualization principles include choosing the right chart type for your data, minimizing chart junk, using color intentionally, and always labeling clearly. Bar charts work well for comparisons. Line charts show trends over time. Simple infographics can communicate key findings at a glance. Report writing should lead with key findings and recommendations. Use plain language and avoid jargon. Include quotes from participants to bring data to life. Visual hierarchy guides the reader through the document. Always contextualize your findings: what do the numbers mean in the real world? What actions do they suggest?

title: Building a Culture of Learning
summary: Organizational strategies for embedding continuous learning and evaluation into everyday practice. Discusses leadership buy-in, staff capacity building, and creating systems that support reflection and adaptation.
transcript: A learning organization is one that continually expands its capacity to create the results it truly desires. Building this culture requires intentional effort at every level. Leadership buy-in is essential: when executives model curiosity and reflection, staff follow. Regular learning moments such as after-action reviews, reflection meetings, and data review sessions help teams pause and learn from experience. Capacity building means investing in staff skills around data literacy, evaluation thinking, and facilitation. Consider designating learning champions in each department. Systems and structures support learning culture: shared data dashboards, regular reporting cycles, and documentation practices all contribute. Psychological safety is critical: staff must feel safe sharing what is not working without fear of blame. Adaptive management means using what you learn to adjust programs in real time rather than waiting until the end of a grant cycle.

title: Equity in Evaluation Practice
summary: An exploration of how equity and inclusion principles can be embedded throughout the evaluation cycle, from question design to dissemination. Covers culturally responsive evaluation frameworks and community-engaged approaches.
transcript: Equity in evaluation requires us to examine who benefits from evaluation, whose knowledge counts, and who bears the burden of data collection. Culturally responsive evaluation recognizes that culture is central to evaluation practice. It means designing evaluation processes that are respectful of and relevant to the cultural context of the program and its participants. Community-engaged evaluation involves community members as partners in the evaluation, not just subjects of it. Participatory approaches give communities voice and agency. Disaggregating data by race, gender, income, and other dimensions allows us to see who is and is not being served equitably. Intersectionality recognizes that people hold multiple identities that shape their experiences. Power dynamics in evaluation: traditional evaluation often positions the evaluator as the expert and community members as data sources. Equitable evaluation flips this relationship. Dissemination with an equity lens means sharing findings back with communities in accessible formats.

title: Designing Surveys That Work
summary: A practical deep-dive into survey design, covering question types, response scales, order effects, and how to increase response rates. Includes common mistakes and how to avoid them.
transcript: Good survey design is both a science and an art. This session covers the mechanics of creating surveys that produce reliable, valid data. Question types include closed-ended, open-ended, Likert scales, ranking, and matrix questions. Each has appropriate uses. Likert scales typically use five or seven response options from strongly disagree to strongly agree. Avoid leading questions, loaded language, and double negatives. Double-barreled questions ask two things at once and should always be split. Question order matters: start with easy questions, group related topics, and put sensitive questions near the end. Response rates: keep surveys short, explain the purpose, send reminders, offer incentives when appropriate, and make surveys mobile-friendly. Pilot testing with a small group before full deployment catches problems early. Cognitive interviewing asks respondents to think aloud while answering, revealing confusion or misinterpretation. Translation and back-translation procedures ensure survey validity in multilingual contexts.

title: Outcome Measurement Fundamentals
summary: How to identify, define, and measure meaningful program outcomes. Covers the difference between outputs, outcomes, and impact, and how to select appropriate indicators for each level.
transcript: Outcome measurement is at the heart of demonstrating program effectiveness. Outputs are the direct products of program activities: number of people served, workshops delivered, or materials distributed. Outcomes are the changes in knowledge, skills, attitudes, behaviors, or conditions that result from the program. Impact refers to the longer-term, broader changes in community or systems. Indicators are measurable expressions of outcomes. A good indicator is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound. Selecting indicators: consider what data you can realistically collect, what your theory of change predicts will change, and what stakeholders care about. Baselines establish the starting point against which change is measured. Setting targets gives you something to compare against. Attribution versus contribution: it is often impossible to claim that your program alone caused an outcome. Contribution analysis is more realistic for most programs. Pre-post designs, comparison groups, and dosage analyses can strengthen causal claims.

title: Focus Groups: From Planning to Analysis
summary: A comprehensive guide to using focus groups as an evaluation tool. Covers recruitment, facilitation techniques, note-taking, and how to analyze and report qualitative data from group discussions.
transcript: Focus groups are a powerful qualitative data collection method that uses group interaction to generate rich data about participants' perspectives, experiences, and opinions. Planning a focus group begins with clear research questions. Who should participate? Recruit participants who share relevant characteristics but are not too similar, as diversity of experience enriches discussion. Ideal group size is six to ten participants. The discussion guide includes a welcome and ground rules, warm-up questions, key questions, and closing questions. Facilitation skills: a good facilitator creates psychological safety, draws out quiet voices, manages dominant participants, and follows up with probing questions. Note-taking: always record with consent and have a separate note-taker so the facilitator can focus on the group. Analysis: transcribe recordings, code data thematically, look for patterns and divergent views. Member checking involves sharing preliminary findings with participants for feedback. Reporting focus group findings: use direct quotes to illustrate themes, contextualize findings, and be transparent about limitations.

title: Funder Reporting and Communication
summary: Practical guidance on reporting evaluation findings to funders, including how to frame challenges and failures honestly, showcase learning, and maintain strong funder relationships through transparent communication.
transcript: Funder reporting is both a compliance requirement and a relationship-building opportunity. Understanding funder priorities: read the grant guidelines carefully and align your reporting to funder questions. Most funders want to know what you did, who you served, what changed, and what you learned. Reporting on challenges and failures honestly builds trust. Funders increasingly expect grantees to share what is not working and what they are doing about it. Adaptive management narratives demonstrate organizational learning capacity. Data presentation in reports: use visuals where possible, highlight key findings, and provide narrative context for numbers. The one-page executive summary is often the most-read section. Relationship management: communicate proactively, not just at required reporting intervals. If something goes wrong, let your program officer know early. Site visits are opportunities to show your work in action. Learning conversations with funders can shift the relationship from compliance to partnership.

title: Building Your Evaluation Plan
summary: A step-by-step walkthrough of creating a comprehensive evaluation plan for a program or initiative. Covers all components including evaluation questions, methods, timeline, roles, and budget considerations.
transcript: An evaluation plan is a roadmap that describes how you will conduct your evaluation. It ensures that evaluation is intentional, systematic, and feasible. Components of an evaluation plan: program description and theory of change, evaluation questions, evaluation design and methods, data sources and collection procedures, analysis approach, roles and responsibilities, timeline, and budget. Evaluation questions should be answered within the available time and resources. They should matter to key stakeholders. Prioritize: you cannot answer every possible question. Mixed methods combine quantitative and qualitative approaches for a fuller picture. Data management planning: how will data be stored, who will have access, and how will confidentiality be protected? Realistic timelines account for recruitment time, data collection, analysis, and reporting. Budgeting for evaluation: staff time is usually the largest cost. Consider whether you need external evaluation support. Stakeholder engagement throughout the evaluation builds buy-in and increases the likelihood that findings will be used. Utilization-focused evaluation keeps the question of use front and center throughout.
